title: Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Judicial Narrowing of Innovation: Analyzing Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner and the Reshaping of the R&D Tax Credit Landscape
subject: Process of Experimentation
summary: Leon Max v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2021-37) is a U.S. Tax Court ruling that denied 100% of the federal R&D tax credits Leon Max claimed through his S corporation, Leon Max, Inc., for 2011 and 2012. The court held that iterative apparel design, fit testing, and fabric quality testing failed the Section 41 qualified research tests.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Context

On March 29, 2021, Judge Ronald L. Buch of the United States Tax Court issued a memorandum opinion in Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37 (Docket No. 20237-16), widely referenced in federal tax practice as Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner. The ruling represents a watershed moment in federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit jurisprudence under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). Addressing a substantial claim arising from the consumer products and apparel sector, the Tax Court systematically dismantled the taxpayer's contention that an iterative, multi-stage commercial garment design and pre-production workflow constituted "qualified research".

The petitioner, Leon Max, was born and raised in Leningrad, Soviet Union (now Saint Petersburg, Russia), and left home at the age of 18 to pursue a career in fashion, making his way to New York City in the 1970s, where he briefly attended the Fashion Institute of Technology before dropping out to move to Los Angeles, where he designed clothes for successful startups and, five years after leaving the Soviet Union, founded his apparel enterprise. Mr. Max served as the sole shareholder, chief executive officer, and creative director of Leon Max, Inc. (LMI), an S corporation engaged in the design, development, production, and sale of women's apparel through department stores throughout the country, its own retail stores, and online. Beginning with an early commercial triumph producing small-sized jumpsuits cut from narrow-width undyed poplin originally used in the manufacture of typewriter ribbons, which Mr. Max and his business partner dyed in fashionable colors—a garment for which no market existed at the time, yet which sold 40,000 units and netted $1 million in LMI's first year—the enterprise expanded into a major fashion house. By the 2011 and 2012 tax years at issue, LMI designed multiple apparel lines tailored to the customer profiles of different department stores—including Max Studio and Studio M for Macy's, Max Studio and Max Studio Specialty Products for Dillard's, Sophie Max for Belk, and the Chelsea and Violet private label owned by Dillard's—as well as its high-end "Leon Max" brand, which catered to women with "discerning taste" and whose higher quality gave the company more flexibility with workmanship, construction, functionality, and creativity. Crucially, although LMI occasionally designed prints and commissioned textile mills to print those designs onto raw fabric, such as silk or georgette, no LMI employee manufactured fabrics in a textile mill during 2011 and 2012.

To transform seasonal design concepts into finished garments ready for retail sale, LMI followed a structured, multistep pre-production development process (which the Court characterized as a nine-step process). This operational sequence began with broad seasonal conceptual planning, thematic ideation, and the assembly of visual mood boards, followed by the creation of design concepts and sketches that designers annotated with detailed descriptions for the patternmakers to follow. Once the sketch was completed, patternmakers worked closely with the designers to draft a first pattern—functioning as a blueprint of the garment's components—after which pattern cutters cut the pattern pieces from the chosen fabric and a sample maker sewed them into a "first sample". LMI then conducted live fitting sessions using a "fit model" who had the same body measurements and proportions as LMI's clothing sample size. During these sessions, the fit model was instructed to position her arms to mimic driving a car, holding a baby, or reaching for an item on a high shelf, as well as to walk on flat surfaces, climb stairs, sit down to assess range of motion, and stand in direct sunlight to verify that the garment was not overly transparent. When range-of-motion or fit issues emerged—such as an inability to sit comfortably in a pair of trousers—patternmakers changed the shape of the crotch and adjusted the fit to the extent the fabric allowed, sometimes requiring a new pattern and sample, and LMI repeated the process until the designer approved the garment. Following these fitting adjustments, LMI produced a "sales sample" to present to retail buyers to secure purchase orders, fabricated a "production prototype" incorporating store feedback and order requirements, and performed marking (laying out pattern pieces on fabric to determine fabric requirements) and grading (adjusting the size-small sample pattern to create medium, large, and extra-large patterns using a digitized grading scale). In the final stage, LMI's third-party manufacturers in China produced a "production approval sample," which LMI reviewed to ensure the factory met all garment criteria (including the correct lining, buttons, zippers, shoulder pads, thread, and fabric) and fit tested before the factory produced the garment; separately, LMI's quality assurance program, overseen by Wayne Friedman, tested fabrics and garments—such as steaming and washing fabric to check for shrinkage, crocking (colorfastness) tests, manually tugging on seams and fabrics to assess strength, and home laundering tests to determine the proper care label—and required every garment to meet these standards before shipment.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Commissioner's Challenge

Following an R&D tax credit study prepared by the consulting firm alliantgroup (which LMI engaged in 2013 and which randomly sampled 35 garments, concluding that 32 involved qualifying activities), LMI filed an amended Form 1120S, U.S. Income Tax Return for an S Corporation, for tax year 2011 claiming $426,255 in Section 41 research credits, and reported $496,462 in research credits on its original 2012 Form 1120S. Because LMI was taxed as a flow-through S corporation, the credits passed through to Mr. Max on his personal income tax returns. Mr. Max amended his 2011 Form 1040 to claim the passthrough of all of LMI's 2011 research credits ($426,255) and, on his 2012 Form 1040, claimed $322,700 of passthrough research credits on Form 3800, General Business Credit, for a combined total of $748,955 across 2011 and 2012. LMI included employee wages, material supplies, and outside contractor costs incurred across its multistep pre-production design and testing workflow as Qualified Research Expenses (QREs).

In June 2016, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue issued a Notice of Deficiency to Mr. Max disallowing 100% of the claimed research credits—$426,255 for 2011 and $322,700 for 2012. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) asserted that LMI's garment development activities represented routine commercial practices typical of the fashion industry, centered on style, taste, cosmetic appearance, and seasonal trends rather than scientific or technological research. Although the opinion does not attribute a separate quality control argument to the Commissioner, the Court ultimately held that LMI's in-house textile testing (such as shrinkage, crocking, pilling, seam strength, and fabric strength tests) constituted quality control testing meant to ensure conformity with established standards, and separately found that fit testing on a model was not investigative in nature.

body.text: Governing Statutory Framework and Final Holding

Under IRC § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer may claim a credit equal to 20% of the excess of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year over a statutory base amount, or alternatively elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(5) as in effect for the 2011 and 2012 tax years (redesignated as § 41(c)(4) in 2018). Pursuant to IRC § 41(b)(1) and (2), QREs encompass in-house research expenses—specifically wages paid to employees for qualified services and costs paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research—along with eligible contract research expenses. Under the foundational principle of Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111 (1933), the Commissioner's deficiency determinations are presumed correct, and the taxpayer bears the burden of proving entitlement to every element of the claimed credit.

To qualify under IRC § 41(d)(1), research activities must be evaluated separately for each discrete business component pursuant to IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(1), and must satisfy a cumulative four-part statutory test. First, under the Section 174 Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A)), the expenditures must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental (R&E) expenses under IRC § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), meaning they represent R&D costs in the experimental or laboratory sense intended to discover information that eliminates uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a product. Second, under the Technological Information Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, which Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4) defines as requiring a process of experimentation that fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)), the taxpayer must intend to apply the discovered information to develop a new or improved business component—defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C)), substantially all (at least 80% under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)) of the research activities must constitute elements of a structured process of experimentation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) conducted for a qualified purpose—defined in IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) as a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, while explicitly excluding activities related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). Moreover, IRC § 41(d)(4) excludes research conducted after commercial production, adaptation or duplication of existing business components, market research, and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control.

Judge Buch ruled in favor of the Commissioner on every contested ground, holding that LMI's garment design and pre-production activities failed the Section 174 Test, the Technological Information Test, and all three sub-elements of the Process of Experimentation Test. Because failing even a single prong of the four-part test is fatal to a research credit claim, the Tax Court declined to address the Business Component Test.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

While the denial of R&D tax credits for clothing design appeared unremarkable on its surface, the Tax Court's sweeping doctrinal analysis in Max v. Commissioner sent shockwaves through the tax controversy community, prompting legal commentators to describe the ruling as a "scorched-earth opinion" that addressed far more than was necessary to disallow the claim. Rather than disposing of the petition narrowly under the statutory exclusion for style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors in IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), Judge Buch erected formidable evidentiary barriers across the Section 174, Technological Information, and Process of Experimentation tests. The ruling exposes five critical legal, technical, and documentation failures that carry broad implications for taxpayers across consumer goods, manufacturing, and engineering industries.
2.1 Failure to Prove Section 174 Objective Technical Uncertainty and the "Investigative" Requirement

To satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), a taxpayer must demonstrate that its claimed expenditures qualify under IRC § 174. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), R&E expenditures are costs incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, aimed at discovering information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Uncertainty exists only if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product.

At trial, Mr. Max contended that LMI confronted pervasive design uncertainties throughout the development of each garment style, specifically pointing to uncertainties regarding how to cut and drape printed fabrics so patterns aligned, which fabrics to select, what thread sizes and gauges to use, how to construct intricate details such as twists, pintucks, and pleating, how to modify and grade patterns for plus-size garments, how fabrics would behave regarding shrinkage during washing, and the final fit of the garment.

The Tax Court dismantled these arguments through a two-fold legal analysis. First, citing Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, 97 T.C.M. (CCH) 1207, at 1255, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Court emphasized that to prove experimental expenditures, a taxpayer must demonstrate that it does not already possess information that can address a capability or method for improving or designing the product, and that its activities were specifically directed toward eliminating those uncertainties. In Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, the Tax Court held that a taxpayer lacked Section 174 uncertainty when it ran its pulsewave machine at 5,000 RPM because it had previously tested the machine at 5,000 RPM and therefore already knew the consequences of doing so. Applying this principle, Judge Buch found that LMI had previously encountered many of the "uncertainties" it faced in 2011 and 2012, and that its employees knew how to align prints, alter standard patterns for the plus-size line, fit garments, and cut fabrics along the proper grain—tasks so routine that LMI required new employees to prove they could accomplish them before being permanently hired. Because the proper thread size for a particular fabric and the proportions of a garment were well known and understood by LMI's designers and patternmakers, and because, even where how to drape a particular fabric to achieve the desired aesthetic was unknown, LMI's garment makers already had the information necessary to address that unknown, these issues did not constitute Section 174 uncertainty.

Second, the Tax Court relied on Mayrath v. Commissioner, 41 T.C. 582, 590 (1964), aff'd, 357 F.2d 209 (5th Cir. 1966), for the proposition that IRC § 174 is intended to limit deductions strictly to expenditures of an "investigative nature" used to develop the concept of a model or product, whereas expenses incurred in the "actual construction" of the product are not investigative in nature and fail to qualify. Applying the Merriam-Webster definition of "investigate" (to observe or study by close examination and systematic inquiry), Judge Buch concluded that LMI's activities—such as cutting and draping fabric to see how it worked, marking and aligning printed fabric, trying thread sizes until one worked, steaming or washing fabric to test shrinkage, tugging on fabric to test durability, and observing a fit model and listening to her feedback—did not involve systematic inquiry or close examination and were common solutions to common problems rather than investigative research.

From a technical tax advisory standpoint, the Court's synthesis of Mayrath and Union Carbide creates severe doctrinal tension with the governing Treasury Regulations. As tax litigators have observed, Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 (adopted in 1994 and revised in 2014) does not contain the words "investigative" or "investigate," and explicitly provides that uncertainty exists when the appropriate design of a product is unknown, even if the general capability and method of construction are established. Similarly, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) eliminated the historic "discovery test" by confirming that entitlement to the research credit does not require scientists or engineers to expand "common knowledge" beyond their professional training. However, Max v. Commissioner illustrates a critical litigation reality: when a taxpayer attempts to dress up routine, skilled design execution (such as selecting thread thickness or adjusting seam allowances) as "appropriate design uncertainty," the Tax Court will invoke Mayrath's "investigative" hurdle and the taxpayer's existing baseline of common professional knowledge to strike down the claim under Section 174.
2.2 Disqualification Under the Quality Control and Routine Testing Exclusion

To substantiate that its pre-production workflow involved experimental testing, LMI pointed to its battery of in-house textile tests, which included steaming and washing fabric samples to determine shrinkage, crocking (colorfastness) and dye tests, pilling tests, home laundering tests to determine the proper care label, and manually tugging on seams and fabric to evaluate strength. Mr. Max argued that this testing fell within the category of "testing to determine if the design of the product is appropriate" and was thus not quality control, citing Field Service Advice memorandum FSA 200013013 concerning a medical device manufacturer—which the Court noted is not precedent.

The Tax Court rejected this argument by enforcing the statutory and regulatory exclusions for quality control under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)(i). Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(3) mandates that research or experimental expenditures do not include costs for the ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control, which Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) defines as testing or inspection to determine whether particular units of material or products conform to specified parameters. The Court found that the goal of LMI's in-house textile testing was quality control: LMI had established parameters that textiles must meet to be used in its garments, followed its own guidelines on pilling, shrinkage, seam strength, and fabric strength, and followed crocking and shrinkage guidelines from the ASTM, the AATCC, the FTC, and the Consumer Product Safety Commission; the tests were standardized, regular, and conducted to ensure the textiles conformed to specific metrics, and fabrics that failed were not used. The Court did not classify fit testing as quality control testing; instead, in its Section 174 analysis, it held that fit testing a garment on a model—while necessary to develop clothing women want to buy and wear—was not investigative in nature because it simply required observing the model and listening to her feedback.
2.3 Failure of the Technological Information Test and the "Hard Sciences" Mandate

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), an activity is qualified research only if it is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is "technological in nature". Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature only if the process of experimentation used to discover such information "fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science".

Mr. Max contended that LMI fundamentally relied on science and engineering—arguing that fit testing relied on engineering, fabric draping and fabric print alignment relied on material sciences, and fabric shrinkage and colorfastness tests relied on chemistry. Consulting Merriam-Webster definitions of engineering, materials science, and chemistry, and reiterating an analogy the Court had used during closing argument, Judge Buch rejected LMI's assertions through the now-famous "baseball centerfielder analogy". The Court noted that while a formula undoubtedly exists to calculate where a spherical projectile launched at a particular speed and angle will land, that does not make a centerfielder a mathematician; rejecting Mr. Max's attempt to distinguish LMI as using such principles to actively overcome uncertainty, the Court held that, as with the centerfielder, science operated in the background of LMI's activities without its employees actually implementing and relying on that science.

Applying this analogy to LMI's workshop, the Court held that receiving feedback from a fit model and then enlarging too-tight armholes or creating more room in a pant leg is neither applying the properties of matter and the sources of energy in nature nor the design and manufacture of complex products such as bridges, satellites, or computers, and thus is not engineering; likewise, draping fabric and aligning fabric patterns did not employ materials science—LMI did not use draping coefficients or indicate knowledge of their existence, and aligning prints requires practice and eyesight rather than science. Similarly, addressing LMI's claim that fabric shrinkage and care testing relied on chemistry, Judge Buch wrote that using chemistry "implies fundamentally changing the structure or composition of materials; washing fabric to determine whether it is prone to shrinkage is not that". Because LMI's shrinkage testing merely observed whether fabric shrank after steaming with a commercial clothes iron or washing and drying in commercial machines, rather than changing the structure or composition of materials, it was not chemistry, and LMI failed the Technological Information Test.
2.4 Collapse of the Process of Experimentation Test: Scientific Method, Style/Taste Exclusion, and the "Substantially All" (80%) Rule

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), a taxpayer must prove that substantially all of the research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Following Union Carbide Corp., 97 T.C.M. (CCH) at 1255, the Tax Court analyzed the Process of Experimentation Test across three mandatory elements—the "qualified purpose" element, the "process of experimentation" (scientific method) element, and the "substantially all" element—concluding that LMI failed every single one.

First, regarding the qualified purpose element, IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) requires that research relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Conversely, IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) explicitly disqualifies any research relating to "style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors". Because LMI's purpose was to create beautiful clothing that women would want to buy—with clothing lines tailored to customer demographics, regional tastes, seasons, and holidays, and with efforts focused on aesthetics such as aligning fabric prints, aligning pintucks, and determining the number of pleats to keep a garment from appearing bulky—the Court held that LMI's design and creation activities were largely driven by style, taste, cosmetic, and seasonal design factors barred by IRC § 41(d)(3)(B); although patternmaking and fit testing served dual functional and aesthetic purposes, Mr. Max provided no evidence to differentiate the costs associated with the aesthetic versus the functional aspects.

Second, regarding the process of experimentation element, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) requires a structured process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset. Citing Union Carbide, the Court held that the uncertainty required for a process of experimentation is essentially identical to Section 174 uncertainty, and that the taxpayer must employ the scientific method—specifically requiring a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the resulting data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense. The Court found that LMI did not employ a process akin to the scientific method: although LMI's nine-step process required care and diligence, each garment that passed through it was not an experiment but a thorough integration of a creative development process; the team understood it could create a sketched dress even without initially knowing its final measurements, elastic heft, or trims; and discerning the proper number and size of pleats, while requiring time and skill, was not a high technology activity rooted in the hard sciences.

Third, regarding the "substantially all" arithmetic element, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) mandates that at least 80% of a taxpayer's research activities for each discrete business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Stated algebraically for any discrete business component :

Relying on Union Carbide and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) (the opinion cites Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, decided just weeks earlier, only for the separate proposition that resolving uncertainty does not necessarily require experimentation), the Tax Court held that because many of LMI's activities were not for a qualified purpose, relating to style, taste, and seasonal design factors, and even its nondisqualified activities did not undergo a process of experimentation, LMI failed to prove that substantially all (at least 80%) of its activities constituted a process of experimentation.
2.5 Substantiation, Aggregation, and the Failure to Invoke the Shrink-Back Rule

Under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), a taxpayer claiming the research credit must maintain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. Furthermore, IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(1) require taxpayers to apply the four-part test separately to each discrete business component. When a top-level product (such as an entire garment or machine) fails the four-part test—typically because non-qualifying design, aesthetic, or commercial production activities dilute the 80% "substantially all" ratio—Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) directs the taxpayer to apply the shrink-back rule. Under the shrink-back rule, the four-part test is reapplied to the most significant subset of elements of the product (and progressively smaller sub-components) until either a qualifying sub-component satisfies all four tests or the most basic element fails.

In Max v. Commissioner, Mr. Max never argued that the shrinking-back rule applied, and the Court expressly declined to apply it on his behalf. The claim was instead built on alliantgroup's study of 35 randomly sampled garments, each evaluated across LMI's entire multistep pre-production process, and the Court noted that Mr. Max provided no evidence to differentiate the costs associated with the aesthetic versus the functional aspects of patternmaking or fit testing. Even if a specific textile treatment or specialized structural element had involved genuine technical uncertainty, the record contained no cost evidence isolating that subset from routine sketching, pattern cutting, sales sample assembly, and quality assurance, and the Court would not apply the shrink-back rule absent an argument from the taxpayer. Although the Max opinion did not cite Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, aff'd, 312 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2002), relied on Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, only for the four-part test and its prior-testing uncertainty example, and did not address any partial allowance under Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), the Court—having held that none of LMI's activities constituted qualified research—disallowed the credits in full.

The following Markdown table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement examined in Max v. Commissioner against the taxpayer's specific failure and the controlling legal standard enforced by the United States Tax Court.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

While Max v. Commissioner confirmed that conventional apparel design falls outside the ambit of IRC § 41, the Tax Court's expansive holdings regarding Mayrath "investigative" expenses, "common knowledge" under Union Carbide, quality control testing exclusions, the "centerfielder analogy," and the 80% "substantially all" ratio create acute audit exposure for legitimate industrial and consumer-goods innovators across the United States. Domestic manufacturers in technical textiles, protective equipment, ergonomic hardware, and specialty consumer products routinely embed authentic chemical and mechanical engineering inside broader commercial pre-production pipelines.

The following two applied remedial case studies demonstrate step-by-step how United States taxpayers confronting the exact statutory and evidentiary pitfalls identified in Max v. Commissioner can restructure their project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Tax Court's objections and fully satisfy IRC § 41.
Case Study 1: Advanced Technical Apparel & Polymer Textile Engineering
Industry Profile and the Naive Claim Vulnerability Audit

"Apex Thermal Systems, Inc." (Apex) is a domestic C corporation headquartered in Oregon that engineers, manufactures, and distributes extreme-cold-weather mountaineering apparel and industrial arc-flash protective garments. To launch its seasonal "GlacierShield Pro" outerwear collection, Apex executes a 10-step pre-production product development workflow. Embedded within this commercial launch is a genuine material science initiative: Apex's polymer chemists and textile engineers seek to formulate a novel three-layer bonded laminate membrane combining an electrospun polyurethane nanofiber matrix with micro-encapsulated phase-change material (PCM) and a fluorine-free (C0) siloxane durable water repellent (DWR) chemical finish, paired with an ultrasonic welded micro-seam technique.

However, in preparing its initial Section 41 claim, Apex's tax advisor defines the entire "GlacierShield Pro Jacket Line" as the business component and aggregates all employee wages, fabric supplies, and contractor invoices across the entire 10-step pre-production workflow. Consequently, the claim includes seasonal color mood boards, silhouette sketching, base pattern drafting, size grading from Small to 3XL, live fit-model ergonomic wear evaluations, retail buyer sales sample sewing, and post-production wash testing for care-label verification, alongside payments to a third-party textile mill ("MillCo") under standard commercial purchase orders to coat fabric rolls and perform tear-strength inspections.

Under the legal standards established in Max v. Commissioner, an IRS examining agent and the Tax Court would disallow 100% of Apex's claim. By defining the entire jacket line as the business component and bundling aesthetic color mood boards, pattern drafting, size grading, and sales sample sewing with polymer chemistry, non-qualifying style and pre-production tasks consume 68% of total project costs ($595,000 out of $875,000), leaving qualifying experimental activities at just 32.0% and failing the 80% "substantially all" threshold under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Little Sandy Coal. Furthermore, adjusting jacket shoulder seams based on a live fit model's feedback while wearing a climbing harness fails the Technological Information Test under Judge Buch's "centerfielder analogy," while washing completed garment samples to verify shrinkage and care-labeling compliance constitutes excluded quality control testing under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)–(4) rather than experimental chemistry. Finally, standard purchase orders issued to MillCo fail to establish qualified contract research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) or distinguish experimental supplies from commercial production inventory.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Sub-Component Shrink-Back Architecture

To neutralize the 80% "substantially all" dilution trap and the IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) style and taste exclusion, Apex restructures its Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) governance prior to project execution by proactively applying the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Rather than claiming the "GlacierShield Pro Jacket" as the business component, Apex establishes two discrete, standalone technical sub-components in its PLM database: Business Component BC-101 (C0 Siloxane Cross-Linked Polyurethane/PCM Composite Membrane Formula) and Business Component BC-102 (Ultrasonic Welded Micro-Seam Structural Assembly Technique).

Simultaneously, Apex bifurcates its general ledger chart of accounts into two mutually exclusive cost centers. Cost Center 400 (Commercial Apparel Design & Pre-Production) captures 100% of the wages, fabric supplies, and vendor fees associated with seasonal conceptual planning, mood boards, fashion sketches, silhouette draping, pattern drafting, size grading, live fit-model adjustments, retail buyer sales samples, and routine care-label wash inspections. Cost Center 400 is completely excluded from the Section 41 tax credit computation. Conversely, Cost Center 700 (Polymer Chemistry & Thermal Engineering R&D) captures exclusively the labor hours of polymer chemists, chemical engineers, and thermal laboratory technicians mapped directly to BC-101 and BC-102, along with raw chemical precursors and destructive experimental laminate swatches.
Step 2: Rebuilding Technical Documentation to Prove Objective Section 174 Uncertainty

To overcome the Tax Court's reliance on Mayrath v. Commissioner ("investigative nature") and Union Carbide ("information already available to the taxpayer"), Apex mandates a formal Section 174 Technical Uncertainty & Prior Art Dossier at the inception of BC-101 and BC-102. Instead of claiming vague uncertainties regarding "fabric choice, thread thickness, and shrinkage" (which Judge Buch dismissed as known industry parameters), Apex's lead polymer chemist documents an objective thermodynamic and macromolecular design uncertainty. Specifically, the dossier establishes that standard fluorine-free (C0) siloxane water-repellent polymers undergo surfactant migration when thermally laminated to an electrospun polyurethane membrane doped with 25% paraffin-based micro-encapsulated PCM, causing catastrophic inter-layer delamination at peel forces below and degrading Moisture Vapor Transmission Rate (MVTR) below the required at .

To satisfy Union Carbide, the dossier appends an internal database query and technical literature review demonstrating that neither Apex's historical formulation logs nor commercial chemical supplier data sheets establish the cross-linking curing kinetics, blocked isocyanate stoichiometric ratios, or ultrasonic horn weld frequencies required to bond the three-layer matrix without rupturing the PCM micro-capsules. Furthermore, to satisfy Mayrath, the governance charter explicitly restricts BC-101 and BC-102 activities to pre-conceptual investigative material science conducted in a laboratory setting to establish the membrane formula and welding technique prior to any commercial garment pattern cutting or construction.
Step 3: Re-Engineering Third-Party Mill and Testing Contracts

In Max, LMI commissioned textile mills to print its designs on raw fabric and relied on third-party manufacturers in China to produce production approval samples; the Court did not separately analyze contract research because, with none of LMI's activities constituting qualified research, its claimed contract expenses failed along with its wages and supplies. To ensure that payments to MillCo for experimental slot-die coating runs qualify as Contract Research Expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)—and to avoid the funded research exclusion or routine vendor material characterization—Apex replaces its commercial purchase orders with a formal Master Research Services Agreement (MRSA) executed prior to the performance of any work.

In strict compliance with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2) and Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), the MRSA contains three mandatory covenants. First, the agreement specifies that MillCo is engaged solely to execute experimental chemical formulation and slot-die coating trials at the direct engineering instruction and parameter specifications of Apex to resolve BC-101 cross-linking uncertainties. Second, the contract vests exclusive ownership and all substantial rights to all resulting chemical formulations, curing parameters, test data, and intellectual property in Apex under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), prohibiting MillCo from using the technology for other customers. Third, the payment schedule places 100% of the financial risk of technical failure on Apex, stipulating that Apex compensates MillCo on a non-refundable time-and-machine-hour basis regardless of whether the coated experimental laminate delaminates or fails MVTR targets. Additionally, all raw isocyanates, siloxanes, and experimental laminate rolls are ordered under dedicated R&D supply codes, shipped directly to Apex's Oregon thermal laboratory, consumed in destructive physical testing, and prohibited by accounting policy from ever entering commercial garment inventory or sales sample production under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C).
Step 4: Implementing Scientific Method and "Substantially All" (80%) Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy Judge Buch's strict standard for the Technological Information Test—which noted that chemistry "implies fundamentally changing the structure or composition of materials"—and the scientific method mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), Apex institutes a mandatory Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) and quantitative Design of Experiments (DoE) protocol. Each ELN entry documents how the experimental trials alter the molecular cross-linking density and physical pore structure of the polymer composite, capturing exact stoichiometric weight percentages of blocked isocyanate cross-linkers, Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) spectra verifying urethane covalent bond formation, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) pore-size distributions, and ultrasonic weld energy inputs (in Joules).

Every experimental iteration in the ELN enforces the five-step scientific method required by Union Carbide: formulating a quantitative hypothesis (e.g., increasing blocked isocyanate concentration from to at a dwell temperature will elevate peel adhesion above while preserving a mean pore diameter of ); executing controlled slot-die coating and ultrasonic welding trials; capturing quantitative laboratory data (Instron tensile peel curves and Sweating Guarded Hotplate evaporative resistance in per ISO 11092); conducting variance and failure-mode analysis on delaminated swatches; and refining the chemical hypothesis for subsequent retesting. All destructive environmental chamber tests are documented as pre-commercial experimental validation used to choose between competing chemical formulations, completely separated from post-production quality control conformity checks under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)–(4). Finally, polymer chemists log their hours daily against granular PLM task codes tied exclusively to BC-101 and BC-102 hypothesis testing, raising the "substantially all" ratio from 32.0% to 94.6%.

body.text: Case Study 2: Industrial Consumer Products & Ergonomic Mechanical Hardware Manufacturing
Industry Profile and the Naive Claim Vulnerability Audit

"Kinetix Worksystems, LLC" (Kinetix) is a Michigan-based manufacturing enterprise taxed as an S corporation that designs and manufactures commercial ergonomic task seating and mechanical monitor support arms. To develop its flagship "AeroFlex 500" commercial office chair, Kinetix follows an 11-step New Product Introduction (NPI) Stage-Gate process. Within this broader commercial program, Kinetix's mechanical engineers attempt to invent a self-weighing, non-linear glass-fiber-reinforced polyamide leaf-spring synchro-tilt mechanism and an anisotropic auxetic lattice thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) lumbar suspension matrix.

In its unexamined tax filing, however, Kinetix defines the entire "AeroFlex 500 Office Chair" as a single business component and claims wages, prototype materials, and outside tooling vendor costs across all 11 NPI stages. The claimed activities include industrial designers sketching chair silhouettes, selecting upholstery weaves and seasonal colorways, sculpting foam mockups, conducting live human "comfort clinics" where employees sit in prototype chairs, mimic reaching for desk drawers, and provide subjective feedback used to widen armrests or reshape seat cushions, assembling showroom samples for commercial trade shows, and executing routine ANSI/BIFMA X5.1 drop and cyclic durability checks on pre-shipment production units. Additionally, Kinetix claims $400,000 paid to an external injection-molding shop ("MoldTech") for hardened steel molds and initial molded components.

Evaluated under Max v. Commissioner, Kinetix's claim faces total disqualification. Instructing human test subjects to sit in a prototype chair, mimic reaching for a desk drawer, and report whether the posture feels restrictive—followed by widening armrests or altering cushion contours—is the exact mechanical equivalent of LMI's fit model mimicking driving a car or sitting in trousers. Under Judge Buch's "centerfielder analogy," ergonomic alterations guided by human observation and subjective comfort feedback fail the Technological Information Test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4). Furthermore, selecting upholstery colors and sculpting chair silhouettes trigger the IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) exclusion for style, taste, and cosmetic design factors, while assembling trade show samples violates the Mayrath prohibition against non-investigative construction costs. Running standard ANSI/BIFMA conformance checks on production approval units is barred as ordinary quality control testing under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)–(4), and bundling the entire 11-step NPI workflow drives the "substantially all" percentage well below the 80% mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Finally, claiming $400,000 of durable steel production tooling violates the Section 174 pilot model rules under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Sub-Component Shrink-Back Isolation

To insulate its core mechanical engineering research from the commercial industrial design and NPI tasks that proved fatal in Max, Kinetix restructures its Stage-Gate governance to enforce sub-component shrink-back isolation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Kinetix removes the overall "AeroFlex 500 Chair" from its R&D study and defines two discrete mechanical subsystems in its Windchill PLM and Jira engineering tracking platforms: Sub-Component M-201 (Variable-Geometry 35% Glass-Fiber-Reinforced Polyamide-66 [PA66-GF35] Torsion Leaf-Spring Kinematic Mechanism) and Sub-Component M-202 (Anisotropic Auxetic Lattice Thermoplastic Elastomer [TPE] Suspension Matrix).

Through formal accounting controls, Kinetix walls off NPI Stages 1 through 3 (Market Ideation, Industrial Design Sketching, Upholstery and Colorway Selection), Stage 7 (Subjective Human Comfort Clinics), Stage 9 (Trade Show Sales Sample Assembly), and Stages 10 through 11 (Commercial Production Tooling and ANSI/BIFMA Quality Control Certification) into non-qualifying commercial work orders. Only engineering hours and experimental supplies incurred within NPI Stages 4 through 6 and Stage 8 that map directly to Sub-Components M-201 and M-202 are permitted to enter the Section 41 tax credit pool.
Step 2: Rebuilding Technical Documentation to Overcome Mayrath, Union Carbide, and the "Centerfielder" Analogy

To refute any IRS contention that its mechanical design iterations represent routine trial-and-error craftsmanship or known engineering parameters under Union Carbide and Mayrath, Kinetix institutes a mandatory Engineering Design Uncertainty Specification (EDUS) at the kickoff of M-201 and M-202. The EDUS documents why standard mechanical engineering equations and polymer supplier data sheets cannot establish the appropriate structural design of Sub-Component M-201: achieving a self-balancing torque-to-recline-angle curve ( variance ) across occupant weights from to without manual spring tensioning requires coupling a non-linear cam-follower linkage with a tapered PA66-GF35 composite leaf spring. However, shear-induced short-glass-fiber alignment during high-pressure injection molding creates complex anisotropic flexural modulus gradients () across the tapered cross-section, generating localized stress concentrations that exceed the fatigue endurance limit prior to recline cycles.

Crucially, to overcome Judge Buch's "centerfielder" and "fit model" holdings, Kinetix completely eliminates subjective human sit-testing from its R&D substantiation. To evaluate Sub-Component M-202 (the auxetic lattice TPE suspension matrix), mechanical engineers utilize an automated, robotic articulated anthropometric loading fixture instrumented with a 1,024-node capacitive pressure-mapping array and six-axis load cells. Rather than asking a human model whether the seat feels comfortable, engineers apply principles of continuum mechanics and solid-state physics to measure peak ischial tuberosity interface pressure (targeting ), viscoelastic hysteresis energy dissipation (), and negative Poisson's ratio deformation ( under biaxial tensile strain).
Step 3: Restructuring Prototype Tooling Contracts and Quality Control Segregation

To prevent the disallowance of the $400,000 paid to MoldTech under IRC §§ 174 and 41(b), Kinetix overhauls its vendor contracting and supply accounting to comply with the pilot model regulations of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)–(4). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), a "pilot model" is defined as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement. Kinetix legally bifurcates its procurement with MoldTech into two separate contracts executed at distinct project phases:

items: Experimental Aluminum Soft-Tooling & Rheology Trial Agreement ($85,000 — Qualifying R&D Supply / Contract Research): Executed during Stage 5 while the geometry and gate design of M-201 remain uncertain, this contract covers sacrificeable, single-cavity 7075-T6 aluminum soft-insert prototype tooling and experimental molding runs used strictly to test melt-front weld lines, fiber orientation tensors, and flexural fatigue failure modes. The contract explicitly states that the aluminum inserts cannot withstand commercial production volumes, will undergo iterative EDM machining modifications between test shots, and will be physically scrapped and destroyed upon completion of M-201 design validation.

Commercial H13 Hardened Steel Multi-Cavity Production Tooling Contract ($315,000 — Excluded Capital Asset): Executed only after M-201 engineering uncertainty is resolved and the CAD geometry is frozen at Stage 9, this contract covers durable steel production molds. The entire $315,000 expenditure is capitalized as depreciable manufacturing equipment under IRC §§ 263A and 168 and completely excluded from QREs.

body.text: Furthermore, Kinetix enforces a strict contractual and operational boundary between Developmental Destructive Failure Testing and Excluded Quality Control Testing under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)–(4). During Stage 5, M-201 pilot models molded from the aluminum soft tooling are mounted in servo-hydraulic fatigue test rigs instrumented with Rosette strain gauges and cycled to catastrophic structural fracture under overload moments to validate Finite Element Analysis (FEA) stress-tensor predictions. Conversely, Stage 10 ANSI/BIFMA X5.1 drop and durability tests conducted on locked production samples to certify commercial safety compliance are logged to quality assurance cost centers and excluded from the research credit claim.
Step 4: Closed-Loop Scientific Method Traceability and 80% Substantiation

To satisfy the Process of Experimentation Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Union Carbide, Kinetix integrates its Windchill PLM repository with a closed-loop scientific method logging protocol. Every CAD iteration of Sub-Component M-201 (Rev 1.1 through Rev 1.9) is linked in a relational database to five mandatory evidentiary artifacts: (1) a documented engineering hypothesis stating how altering rib taper angle or injection gate geometry will modify the glass-fiber orientation tensor and reduce peak von Mises stress; (2) Moldflow computational fluid dynamics (CFD) polymer rheology simulations and ANSYS structural FEA outputs; (3) physical servo-hydraulic strain-gauge micro-strain () and cycles-to-failure datasets from the aluminum soft-tool pilot models; (4) quantitative regression analysis diagnosing variance between predicted FEA stress and observed physical fracture loci; and (5) documented geometric refinements for the subsequent hypothesis test. Engineers record their hours contemporaneously against specific M-201 and M-202 experimental iteration codes, ensuring that over 91% of all tracked costs on each shrunk-back sub-component constitute direct elements of a scientific process of experimentation.

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis for United States Tax Practitioners

The United States Tax Court's ruling in Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37, carries jurisprudential weight that extends far beyond the apparel and fashion industry. Read in concert with Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, Max cements a rigorous judicial enforcement paradigm for federal Section 41 R&D tax credit claims. Taxpayers and technical tax advisors can no longer rely on broad narratives describing iterative commercial product development workflows—whether termed "pre-production," "New Product Introduction," or "multi-stage design"—to satisfy the statutory four-part test.

To withstand IRS examination and Tax Court litigation under the standards established by Judge Buch, domestic taxpayers must embed four structural safeguards into their R&D tax credit governance. First, taxpayers must abandon holistic workflow aggregation in favor of proactive sub-component isolation under the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), anchoring claims exclusively at the level of discrete chemical formulations, mechanical subsystems, or manufacturing processes so that aesthetic styling, market adaptation, and sales sample construction never enter the business component definition. Second, taxpayers must establish a clear evidentiary boundary between hard-science experimentation and visual or ergonomic craftsmanship; because the Max Court held that fit testing based on observing a model and listening to her feedback was not investigative, did not apply engineering principles under the "centerfielder analogy," and served dual aesthetic and functional purposes whose costs Mr. Max never differentiated (implicating the IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) style and taste exclusion), documentation must highlight quantitative engineering simulations, analytical physics, or molecular material alterations. Third, taxpayers must strictly segregate experimental hypothesis validation from ordinary quality control testing, ensuring that post-design verification against commercial, safety, or care-labeling parameters is excluded under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)–(4) and IRC § 41(d)(4)(D). Finally, taxpayers must protect the 80% "substantially all" arithmetic calculation of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) through granular project time-tracking and bifurcated cost accounting, ensuring that every claimed business component is supported by a verifiable, hypothesis-driven record of scientific experimentation.
